messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Gerald is a 78-year-old divorced man who works as a database administrator, a role he has held for decades and continues to perform remotely from the home office he built into the back bedroom of his house in suburban Ohio. Fourteen months ago, Gerald was admitted to the intensive care unit following a rapid deterioration from what had initially presented as a respiratory infection. Within forty-eight hours he was intubated, and for eleven days he lay sedated and ventilated, his body sustaining itself on machines while his physicians told his adult daughter, who drove through the night to reach him, that the outcome was uncertain. Gerald has no continuous memory of those eleven days, but what he does retain is fragmentary and grotesque: the sensation of something forcing air into his lungs against his will, a smell — antiseptic and something beneath it, something organic and wrong — that he cannot name but cannot escape, and a moment of partial consciousness in which he understood, with a clarity he describes as unlike anything he had known before, that he was very close to dying. He recovered. He was discharged. And then, over the weeks that followed, something that should have felt like relief instead became the architecture of a new kind of suffering.

Gerald returned home to find that home no longer felt safe. Even now, seated at his workstation running queries and monitoring server logs — tasks he has performed with quiet competence for thirty years — he finds himself pausing to listen, scanning the room without knowing what he is scanning for, his body held at a low-level readiness that never fully releases. He feels on guard inside his own house, watchful in a way that exhausts him by evening and that he cannot rationalize away despite knowing, intellectually, that no threat is present. The fear is not located in a thought he can argue with. It is located in his body, which he has come to regard with something close to betrayal. He had believed, as many people do implicitly, that his body was a reliable instrument. The illness dissolved that belief entirely, and now when his heart rate rises or his breathing feels shallow, he interprets these signals not as ordinary fluctuation but as evidence of ongoing danger — his body reacting as though the ICU is still happening, as though the crisis never resolved. This persistent physiological alertness feeds directly into a broader sense that the world itself is not safe, that danger is not an exceptional event but a structural feature of existence, and that he was simply naïve not to have seen this before.

What makes Gerald's presentation particularly tenacious is the quality of his intrusive memories. When the recollection surfaces — triggered sometimes by nothing he can identify, sometimes by a clinical smell encountered in a pharmacy or a doctor's waiting room — it does not arrive as a memory in the ordinary sense. It arrives as a present-tense event. He smells what he smelled in the ICU. He feels the weight of the ventilator's rhythm. He is, for those seconds, not a man sitting at a desk in Ohio but a man dying in a hospital bed, and the vividness of this experience exceeds anything in his ordinary memory, as though the event burned itself into him at a different depth than the rest of his life. These episodes do not leave him frightened and then settled. They leave him frightened and then confirmed — confirmed in what his hypervigilance already insists upon, that the threat is real and present, that his body cannot be trusted, that the world is a place where catastrophe arrives without warning and without mercy. He has lost whatever faith he once held in the orderliness of things, in the idea that a person who takes reasonable care will be reasonably protected. His divorce, years behind him, had already loosened his connections to others, but since the illness he has withdrawn further, canceling the occasional dinners with colleagues he once maintained, declining his daughter's invitations. He had come to believe, without quite articulating it, that closeness to others was simply another form of exposure to loss.

Gerald sought help after his daughter found him, during a routine video call, visibly shaking and unable to explain why. What he most wants, he said at intake, is to feel like himself again. What he most fears is that the man he was before the ICU no longer exists to return to.
